title: Jeremiah 31:23–30
context: The LORD of Armies promises that the old blessing will be spoken again in Judah when he reverses their captivity: “The LORD bless you, habitation of righteousness, mountain of holiness” (31:23), with farmers and shepherds dwelling together and every weary soul satisfied (31:24–25). In 31:26 the first-person voice says, “On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me.” Many readers hear Jeremiah describing how this vision of hope came to him, perhaps in a dream or trance; others take the line as a figure for the refreshment the message brought. The text does not say more. In 31:27–28 the LORD promises to sow Israel and Judah with the seed of man and animal and to watch over them to build and plant, as he once watched over them to pluck up and destroy; the verbs echo, with different wording, the commission of 1:10. In 31:29–30 the proverb “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” will no longer be said, because everyone will die for his own iniquity. Ezekiel 18 cites the same proverb and develops the theme at length; Deuteronomy 24:16 and the warnings of Exodus 20:5 and 34:7 are often read alongside it. Both traditions affirm personal accountability here, and neither treats the verse as denying the solidarity of the human race in sin (compare Romans 5:12). The site’s existing discussion at 1 Timothy 2:4 covers the wider question of God’s saving desire, and no new contrast is added here.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Yet again they will use this speech in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I reverse their captivity: ‘The LORD bless you, habitation of righteousness, mountain of holiness.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies promises that Judah will again say, “The LORD bless you, habitation of righteousness, mountain of holiness.” Arminian readers see the restoration of worship and blessing in Jerusalem, a city once condemned for injustice now called righteous and holy as its people live in renewed faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD himself giving the city a new name and character, so righteousness and holiness are his gifts to a restored people. Shared ground: both traditions read the blessing as a reversal of the city’s former shame (compare 7:4–11), and both see “when I reverse their captivity” tying the promise to God’s act of restoration.

verses.text: Judah and all its cities will dwell therein together, the farmers, and those who go about with flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: “Judah and all its cities will dwell therein together, the farmers, and those who go about with flocks.” Arminian readers see peaceful community restored, with farmers and herders living side by side, and they note that ordinary work becomes part of the blessing of a people living under God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same peaceful scene as the fruit of God’s restoring grace, which reaches the whole land and every kind of life in it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as settled, ordinary life after war and exile, and both see the harmony of farmers and shepherds as a picture of covenant peace.

verses.text: For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.”
verses.arminianNotes: “For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.” Arminian readers hear God’s compassion for the exhausted and grieving, offered to every sorrowful soul, and they see refreshment as the experience of those who come to him in their need (compare Matthew 11:28).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same promise stated as accomplished, “I have satiated,” and see it as the certainty of God’s grace toward his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the weariness and sorrow as the aftermath of judgment, and both see the LORD himself as the one who restores the soul (compare Psalm 23:3).

verses.text: On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me.” Arminian readers, with many others, hear Jeremiah describing the refreshment of receiving a message of hope after so many oracles of judgment. Whether the revelation came in a dream or the line is figurative is uncertain, and the verse does not settle it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the prophet’s relief and joy at a word of restoration, and they note how unusual a sweet sleep is in a book filled with anguish (compare 4:19). Shared ground: both traditions hold the manner of revelation loosely, and both read the verse as showing that the promise brought real comfort to the prophet himself.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of animal.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of animal.” Arminian readers see God repopulating a desolate land, reversing the emptiness of judgment, and they note that both houses are again included in the promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the sower, with growth and life coming from his sovereign blessing, and they hear an echo of creation’s fruitfulness in the renewal of the land. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reversal of the desolation threatened earlier (compare 4:25–26; 33:10–12), and both see Israel and Judah reunited in God’s purpose.

verses.text: It will happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so I will watch over them to build and to plant,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down … so I will watch over them to build and to plant.” Arminian readers see God’s watchful attention turning from judgment to restoration as the people receive his discipline, and they note that both actions express his care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same watchfulness as God’s faithful oversight of his purposes, carrying out judgment and restoration alike (compare 1:12). Shared ground: both traditions hear an echo of the commission in 1:10, whose verbs differ in wording, and both see the LORD’s word fulfilled in tearing down and in building.

verses.text: “In those days they will say no more, “ ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’
verses.arminianNotes: The proverb “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” will no longer be said. Arminian readers see the end of a fatalistic excuse that blamed the previous generation, and they stress that each generation is accountable to God and free, by grace, to respond to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the proverb rejected as an evasion of responsibility, while holding that the verse does not deny the solidarity of humanity in sin (compare Romans 5:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with Ezekiel 18, which cites the same proverb, and both affirm personal accountability before God.

verses.text: But everyone will die for his own iniquity. Every man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.
verses.arminianNotes: “But everyone will die for his own iniquity. Every man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.” Arminian readers see personal responsibility affirmed: judgment falls on the one who sins, and so each person is called to turn and live (compare Ezekiel 18:30–32).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same principle of personal accountability, consistent with Deuteronomy 24:16, and they read it within the new covenant context of 31:31–34, where God deals with each person’s heart. Shared ground: both traditions affirm individual responsibility, and the site’s discussion at 1 Timothy 2:4 covers the wider question of God’s saving desire.
